Mount Fuji is Japan's highest peak at twelve thousand three hundred eighty-eight feet, located on the island of Honshu roughly sixty miles west of Tokyo. An iconic symbol of Japanese culture and landscape, it is a dormant stratovolcano that last erupted in seventeen hundred seven through seventeen hundred eight. The distinctive cone shape results from repeated eruptions building a symmetrical profile, making it perhaps the world's most aesthetically recognizable mountain. Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in two thousand thirteen, Mount Fuji is sacred in Shinto tradition as the home of a divine spirit, known as a kami. The climbing season is brief, running from July through September when snow melts and weather is most stable. Thousands of people summit each day during peak season. First ascent records are uncertain, as mythology and history blend together, but organized pilgrimage climbing became a practice by the eleventh century. The mountain features prominently in Japanese art, most famously in Katsushika Hokusai's eighteenth-century print series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. The ascent takes one day for most climbers, and altitude acclimatization is minimal due to its modest height, making it accessible to non-climbers and children.
